passage_text: Researchers studied the impact of acute sleep deprivation on cognitive performance in a controlled laboratory setting. Eight healthy adults (4 males, 4 females) were randomly assigned to either a sleep-deprived group (n=4) or a well-rested control group (n=4). The sleep-deprived group was kept awake for 24 hours, while the control group slept normally. After the intervention, all participants completed a computerized psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) measuring reaction time (RT) and a working memory task assessing accuracy. The study aimed to determine whether lack of sleep impairs reaction speed and memory precision. Data were collected, analyzed, and compared between groups. The researchers hypothesized that sleep deprivation would lead to slower reaction times and lower accuracy. Results indicated that the sleep-deprived group had an average RT of 350 ms and 77.5% accuracy, whereas the control group had an average RT of 282.5 ms and 91.5% accuracy. The findings support the hypothesis that acute sleep loss negatively affects both speed and accuracy in cognitive tasks.
table_data:
Participant | Group | Hours Slept | Reaction Time (ms) | Accuracy (%)
---|---|---|---|---
P1 | Sleep-Deprived | 0 | 360 | 75
P2 | Sleep-Deprived | 0 | 340 | 80
P3 | Sleep-Deprived | 0 | 355 | 77
P4 | Sleep-Deprived | 0 | 345 | 78
P5 | Control | 8 | 280 | 92
P6 | Control | 7 | 285 | 90
P7 | Control | 8 | 275 | 93
P8 | Control | 7 | 290 | 91
stem: Which participant had the fastest reaction time?
explanation: Participant P7 had the fastest reaction time of 275 ms, which is lower than all other participants listed in the table.
trap: Students may mistakenly select P5 because it is the first control participant, but the fastest RT belongs to P7.

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for individual differences in baseline cognitive ability?

options.D: Administering the tasks at the same time of day

explanation: Random assignment distributes individual differences evenly across groups, thereby controlling for baseline cognitive ability.
trap: Students might think that administering tasks at the same time controls for circadian effects, but the key control for individual differences is random assignment.

stem: Which statement is FALSE based on the data presented?

options.A: The sleep-deprived group had a higher average reaction time than the control group.
options.B: All control participants slept at least 7 hours.
options.C: Participant P1 had the lowest accuracy among the sleep-deprived group.
options.D: Participant P5 had the fastest reaction time of all participants.

explanation: Correct: D) P5's reaction time was 280 ms, but P7 was faster at 275 ms, so the statement is false. Why the others are wrong: A) The deprived mean (350 ms) exceeds the control mean (282.5 ms), so it is true. B) Control participants slept 7 or 8 hours, so it is true. C) P1 scored 75%, lower than P2 (80%), P3 (77%) and P4 (78%), so it is true.
trap: Students may assume the first control participant automatically has the fastest RT, but the data shows otherwise.

stem: Which feature of this study most limits how confidently the results can be generalized?

options.A: Only eight participants were tested, four per group.
options.B: Participants were randomly assigned to groups.
options.C: Both reaction time and accuracy were measured.
options.D: A well-rested control group was included.

explanation: Correct: A) With four participants per group, the group means are imprecise and may not represent a larger population. Why the others are wrong: B) Random assignment is a strength of the design. C) Measuring two outcomes does not limit generalizability. D) A control group is needed to attribute differences to sleep loss.
trap: Choosing random assignment (option B) as a limitation; it strengthens the comparison, whereas the tiny sample size restricts generalization.
